narrative:
The model predicts you have a 13% chance of failing your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your reason for choosing this school, your past academic record, and your ambition to pursue higher education. Surprisingly, the top influence worked in your favor: choosing the school because it is close to home pushed the prediction toward passing. This is a positive factor shared by about a quarter of students who ultimately succeeded.

However, two other important elements pulled the outcome the other way. Although you have had no previous class failures (matching the average of students who passed), the model still sees this absence of prior setbacks as less reassuring than it does for other students. More critically, while you have a clear desire to continue into higher education (something every successful student in the data also expressed), the model weighed this ambition as providing weaker protection for you than it does for most peers. Together these influences tipped the balance just enough to flag a risk of failure.

To improve, focus on turning your motivation for higher education into concrete daily study habits and consider using the remedial courses to close any small gaps before they grow. Small, consistent effort now can remove the need for extra classes next year. (218 words)
